{%with bg="/media/report/image4.png"%} {% endwith %} General Recommendations

1. Survey the occupants twice a year (early summer and early winter) regarding thermal comfort. The space may be over-conditioned (too cool in the summer and/or too warm in the winter) unnecessarily. 

2. Implementing or adjusting an unoccupied (“fallback”) temperature setpoint by even a fraction of a degree above the occupied setpoint (during summer) or below the occupied setpoint (during winter) can yield energy savings without impacting occupant comfort.

3. Perimeter spaces are typically more challenging to accurately condition due to solar loading. Use blinds or curtains where possible to mitigate this effect (open in winter and closed in summer).  

4. Opening doors to non-private offices, meeting rooms, and similar spaces at the end of the day improves ventilation and helps the building perform efficiently. 

5. Ensure that the ventilation system engages approximately two hours prior to occupancy to assist in improving ventilation rates and overall air quality.

Accuracy

Description

The temperature differential is the temperature difference between when the heating or cooling system engages and disengages. Typical thermostat temperature differentials range from 0.5°C to 2°C (~1°F to ~3°F).

Analysis

The percentage of time the space was within 0.5°C, 1°C, and 2°C (~1°F, ~2°F, ~3°F) from the setpoint temperature (if provided) or the average temperature was analyzed. Although there is no single, ideal temperature differential value, this analysis highlights how locations within the space perform with respect to each other. The National Energy Code 9.36.3.6 states that the temperature of a space should not vary more than 0.5°C (1°F) from the setpoint temperature to maximize efficiency; however, many systems are set to a 2°C temperature differential by default.

Guide on How to Read the Graph

Locations are indicated on the horizontal axis, and percentage of time within the temperature differential value is on the vertical axis. The figure is divided into three sections based on the three temperature differential values, 0.5°C, 1°C, and 2°C (~1°F, ~2°F, ~3°F).

Consistency

{% comment %}

{% endcomment %}

Description

Temperature is the primary variable used to control a building’s heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system (HVAC). Thermostats measure the current temperature of a space and compare that to a setpoint value. A measured temperature above the setpoint in a warm external environment (i.e. summer) will trigger a call for cooling to reduce the temperature, and the reciprocal is true for a cool environment (i.e. winter). Buildings are typically divided into zones to accommodate similar loads. For example, computer rooms that generate more heat would be zoned separately from cubicles or offices that typically generate less heat.

Analysis

The purpose of this analysis was to identify the number of unique thermal performance clusters per floor. Each cluster represents a group of sensors that measured statistically similar temperature trends over time. While not identical, each cluster illustrates the sensors and locations that responded similarly to weather and the HVAC system consistency.

We measured how consistently the HVAC equipment is controlling the temperature of the building.

Guide on How to Read the Graph

Locations (sensors) that share a colour followed statistically similar temperature trends over time. Similar clusters are a result of similarly conditioned air flow and ventilation, occupancy or space use, weather, as well as solar loading.

{%with bg="/media/report/image4.png"%} {% endwith %} Are Thermostat Setpoints Optimized?

Description

An efficient building should not always maintain a single, constant temperature. During unoccupied hours a “fallback” temperature can be scheduled, allowing the building to be cooler in the winter and warmer in the summer than during occupied hours. This strategy can decrease total energy consumption without compromising occupancy comfort.

Analysis

This analysis illustrates the temperature performance of the tested locations over the course of an average day. It highlights trends rather than discrete events, revealing the general temperature distribution by location of the testing building. It can be used to more accurately schedule a fallback temperature based on occupancy. The following figure is an example of a temperature setpoint schedule:

{% with bg="/media/report/image8.png" %} {% endwith %}  Are Building Occupants Comfortable?

Description

Acceptable temperature and humidity ranges are defined in building code standards and are designed to keep occupants comfortable. The comfortable range is determined by factors such as clothing insulation, activities performed within the space, and local climate. Buildings conditioned within the comfortable range experience fewer tenant complaints, reduced illness rates, and increased productivity.

Analysis

For the purpose of this analysis, a comfortable space is defined by ASHRAE 55-2017. Generally, this range is between 18°C and 23°C (~64°F and ~73°F) based on typical commercial office occupancy, activities, and clothing insulation. Measurements were made to determine whether the building is conditioned to levels generally considered comfortable for its occupants during occupied hours.

Guide on How to Read the Graph

The locations where measurements were recorded are labeled on the horizontal axis. The average percentage of the occupied time period that each location was within the comfortable range is labeled on the vertical axis. The occupied time period is defined as the time of day when people typically work or reside within the space and when thermal comfort is most critical. It is building dependent and input by the user prior to performing this analysis. The target value is 100%, which means that the corresponding location was comfortable during the entire occupied time period.

Occupant Comfort - Summary

Guide on How to Read the Graph

The average percentage of the occupied time period that each sensor was within the comfortable range is overlaid on a floor plan. The target value is 100%, which means that the corresponding location was comfortable during the entire occupied time period.

{% with bg="/media/report/image12.png" %} {% endwith %} What is the air quality?

Description

The quality of indoor air inside buildings is important for the occupants' comfort and their health. Poor indoor air quality (IAQ) has been tied to sick building symptoms (SBS) such as headaches, fatigue, trouble concentrating, and irritation of the eyes, nose, throat and lungs[1].  

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are compounds that can be emitted by common materials such as paints, flooring, upholstery, and cleaning supplies[2]. Total volatile organic compounds (TVOCs) is a measurement of the total combination of individual VOCs present in the building.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration increases with higher occupancy, and is diluted and removed from buildings based on air ventilation rates. Therefore, examining the level of CO2 in a building in comparison with the occurring level outside the building, can provide information of the building's occupant densities and the effectiveness of the ventilation[3].

Analysis

To analyze the TVOCs and CO2 values, concentrations measured throughout the test period are compared to acceptable exposure thresholds[4]. All buildings, regardless of age or type, should keep TVOC levels as low as possible and minimize their sources. Target indoor CO2 concentrations should be close to outdoor air concentrations. The data presented here can be used to prioritize remediation efforts.


TVOC

{%with bg="/media/report/image17.png" %} {%endwith%}  How Likely is Virus Transmission?

Description

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is an indicator of the ventilation and accompanying infectious particles exhaled by occupants[5]. In typical commercial buildings, occupants are the major source of CO2, so a rise in CO2 indicates that exhaled air is building up in a space. The more exhaled air that is present, the more likely it is for another occupant to encounter infectious particles. Thus, long term CO2 concentrations can indicate areas where infectious particles may linger; occupants using these spaces are at higher risk[6].

Relative humidity is the amount of water vapor present in the air at a given temperature. Low RH can dry out the mucosal membranes in the eyes, nose, mouth, and lungs. These membranes play a vital role in the human immune system and are the first point of contact of many viruses. A dry mucous membrane can render an individual more susceptible to infection. Airborne particles also travel farther and remain suspended for longer in dry air, increasing the risk of infection[7][8]. It is recommended that indoor spaces achieve moderate-range humidity levels; in the case of COVID-19, this is between 40 – 60% relative humidity[7].

Analysis

The virus transmission risk is based on the percent of occupied time that spaces within the building measured desirable carbon dioxide (CO2) and relative humidity (RH) values.

Guide on How to Read the Graph

The locations where measurements were recorded are labeled on the horizontal axis. The average virus transmission prevention score for each tested floor during the occupied time period is labeled on the vertical axis. Higher scores are better, indicating a lower risk of virus transmission.
